summary: Sol Keeper is a free browser game for ages 7 to 12 that trains the thinking behind a real Mars mission: keeping a crew alive. Players run a small outpost on the real ground of Jezero crater, built from the NASA HiRISE terrain map used to land Perseverance. Each sol they have only a few work slots to share between four supplies, oxygen, power, water and food, while daylight, dust storms and radiation change what every choice costs. They drive a rover across the crater, scan machines NASA left on Mars (Perseverance, Spirit, Opportunity and Sojourner) to learn their true stories, and 3D-print upgrades that fix the problems those missions faced. A message to Earth takes as long as it really would today, worked out from JPL orbital elements. The challenge asks for a trainer that makes mission trade-offs tangible and fun; Sol Keeper turns them into play. It runs in any web browser, including school Chromebooks, with no install and no login.
details:
What it does

Sol Keeper is a base-management and exploration game set on Mars. The player is a junior astronaut keeping a small outpost alive on the floor of Jezero crater. One sol (a Mars day) lasts 12 minutes of play. Every choice costs something: printing a part, watering the crops, charging a suit or calling Earth each uses one of a few daily work slots and some of the base's power, water or food. Skipping a meal or staying up past midnight leaves fewer slots for the next day, so players learn to plan ahead the way a real crew must.

How it works

- Four supplies: oxygen, power, water and food. Solar power follows the Sun across the sol and drops with dust and storms; panels must be brushed clean. Oxygen is made from water, the way a crew would make it from ice, and the game explains how NASA's MOXIE made oxygen from the Martian air instead. Crops take time to grow, using growing times from NASA's plant experiments on the ISS.

- Radiation: a suit gauge drops faster at night and much faster during a solar flare, so players learn when to stay inside.

- Explore: drive a rover over real Jezero terrain. Every metre drains the battery the base needs tonight.

- Scan: find the real machines NASA sent to Mars. Each scan unlocks a short film about that machine's true story.

- Upgrade: the Lab reads why a machine failed (for example Opportunity, lost to a dust storm in 2018), and the Workshop 3D-prints the fix, such as a storm mode for the base.

- Earth link: the delay to Earth is calculated for today's date from JPL's planetary orbital elements, so players see that talking to home is not instant.

NASA data in the game

- Terrain: the Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE (1 m) and CTX (20 m) elevation mosaics of western Jezero, cut into three nested grids (1 m, 4 m and 40 m) so the near ground is exact and the crater rim is still visible on the horizon.

- The globe: MOLA global elevation from Mars Global Surveyor.

- Distance and light delay to Earth: Kepler's equation solved for today's date with JPL's published orbital elements.

- Rover models: built from NASA/JPL photos in the NASA Image and Video Library.

- Facts on radiation (Curiosity RAD), oxygen (MOXIE), life support (ECLSS), crew isolation (CHAPEA) and crops (ISS plant experiments) come from NASA pages and are shown in the game with their source.

What is not real data: the weather is a seeded game forecast, not live Mars weather, and we say so.

Benefits and intended impact

Interest in science drops between ages 10 and 14 (TIMSS 2023: 53% of 10-year-olds very much like learning science, 40% of 14-year-olds in integrated science). Sol Keeper lets children feel the trade-offs a real crew faces on ground NASA really mapped, instead of only watching a launch. Because it runs in a browser on low-cost Chromebooks with no account, a teacher can use it in class straight away. Our next steps are a classroom trial in Athlone and a daily challenge seeded from NASA's DONKI space-weather feed.

How it is creative

The game joins real science to play: the ground under your feet is a real NASA map, the machines you find are real missions, and their real failures become the upgrades you build. Every real fact shows its source.

Tools, languages and software

- JavaScript (ES modules, no build step) and Three.js r170 for 3D, with custom GLSL shaders for the cartoon ink outlines.

- HTML, CSS and SVG for the interface; Web Audio for sound; the browser's local storage for saves.

- Python for turning the NASA terrain files into small game grids.

- Node.js and Puppeteer for automated checks.

- Meshy for the 3D models (GLB), and SI video tools for the machine films.

- Hosted on Vercel.

Factors we considered

- Low-cost school hardware: the game picks a lighter graphics level on Chromebooks and weak devices. Measured on a laptop: 60 frames per second, about 3 ms of work per frame, about 35 MB downloaded.

- Honesty: real facts and game rules are kept apart, and every real fact shows where it came from.

- Age: words, goals and controls are set for ages 7 to 12.
